chart.instructions: The input state is a Markdown table from a coding assistant's reply, along with inferred column types. A single chart will be rendered beneath the table, and each candidate option states exactly what that chart plots. Pick the option that communicates most accurately and clearly what the table aims to convey. A valid chart relies on sound comparisons: elements sharing an axis must represent the same kind of quantity, connecting lines or ratios between two values must link matching quantities, and plotted columns should show the measured outcomes a reader compares—never sample counts, configuration parameters, or IDs. Pick none if no option produces a useful comparison, or when the numbers are identifiers, parameters, or too sparse or uniform to benefit from plotting beyond the table itself.

criteria.bar: Bar chart: one bar per {{axis}} showing "{{first}}", each annotated with its value{{#if reference}} and its delta relative to "{{reference}}"{{/if}}.
criteria.paired: {{#if transition}}Dumbbell chart: for each {{axis}}, a segment from its "{{first}}" value to its "{{second}}" value along a common axis (log-scaled when spanning multiple orders of magnitude), annotated with both values and their ratio.{{else}}Dumbbell chart: for each {{axis}}, two connected points for its "{{first}}" and "{{second}}" values along a common axis (log-scaled when spanning multiple orders of magnitude), annotated with both values and their ratio.{{/if}}
criteria.slope: Slope chart: one line per {{axis}} connecting its values across {{#list series prefix='"' suffix='"' join=', '}}{{this}}{{/list}} in sequence.
criteria.grouped: Grouped bars: for each {{axis}}, side-by-side bars for {{#list series prefix='"' suffix='"' join=', '}}{{this}}{{/list}}{{#if moreSeries}} plus {{moreSeries}} more{{/if}} on a common axis.
criteria.stacked: Stacked bars: one bar per {{axis}}, divided into segments for {{#list series prefix='"' suffix='"' join=', '}}{{this}}{{/list}}{{#if whole}} summing to "{{whole}}"{{/if}}{{#if normalized}}, with each bar normalized to 100%{{/if}}.
criteria.line: Line chart: {{#list series prefix='"' suffix='"' join=', '}}{{this}}{{/list}}{{#if moreSeries}} plus {{moreSeries}} more{{/if}} plotted as lines over {{#if x}}"{{x}}"{{else}}the {{axis}} entries in table order{{/if}}.
criteria.heatmap: Heatmap: a matrix of cells with one row per {{axis}} and one column per {{#list series prefix='"' suffix='"' join=', '}}{{this}}{{/list}}{{#if moreSeries}} plus {{moreSeries}} more{{/if}}, displaying each cell's value and shaded accordingly{{#if perColumn}} within each column{{/if}}{{#if perRow}} within each row{{/if}}.
criteria.multiples: {{#if transposed}}Small multiples: one panel per table row ({{#list series prefix='"' suffix='"' join=', '}}{{this}}{{/list}}{{#if moreSeries}} plus {{moreSeries}} more{{/if}}), each comparing {{#list rows prefix='"' suffix='"' join=', '}}{{this}}{{/list}}{{#if moreRows}} plus {{moreRows}} more{{/if}} on an independent scale.{{else}}Small multiples: one panel per column ({{#list series prefix='"' suffix='"' join=', '}}{{this}}{{/list}}{{#if moreSeries}} plus {{moreSeries}} more{{/if}}), each plotting one bar per {{axis}} on an independent scale{{#if reference}}, compared against "{{reference}}"{{/if}}.{{/if}}
criteria.share: Share bar: a single bar divided into each {{axis}}'s proportion of the "{{first}}" total.
criteria.diverging: Diverging bars: one bar per {{axis}} for "{{first}}", extending right for positive values and left for negative values.
criteria.butterfly: Back-to-back bars: for each {{axis}}, "{{first}}" extending left and "{{second}}" extending right from a central axis, with each net value shown alongside.
criteria.scatter: Scatter plot: one marker per {{axis}}, positioned at "{{x}}" along the horizontal axis and "{{first}}" along the vertical axis; no additional columns are plotted.
criteria.change: Factors of change: for each {{axis}}, the multiplier by which {{#list series prefix='"' suffix='"' join=', '}}{{this}}{{/list}}{{#if moreSeries}} plus {{moreSeries}} more{{/if}} {{#if second}}exceed or trail{{else}}exceeds or trails{{/if}} "{{baseline}}", plotted as bars extending from 1×.
criteria.progress: Progress bars: one bar per {{axis}} for {{#list series prefix='"' suffix='"' join=', '}}{{this}}{{/list}}, each filled out of 100%.
criteria.timeline: Timeline: each {{axis}}'s "{{first}}" laid sequentially end to end along one axis in table order.
criteria.waterfall: Waterfall: each {{axis}}'s "{{first}}" accumulated incrementally in table order up to the combined total.
criteria.dots: Dot plot: for each {{axis}}, one marker per {{#list series prefix='"' suffix='"' join=', '}}{{this}}{{/list}}{{#if moreSeries}} plus {{moreSeries}} more{{/if}} along a common axis (log-scaled when spanning multiple orders of magnitude){{#if baseline}}, expressed as multiples of "{{baseline}}"{{/if}}.
criteria.range: Range chart: for each {{axis}}, the min–max span across {{#list series prefix='"' suffix='"' join=', '}}{{this}}{{/list}} rendered as a floating bar.
criteria.bullet: Bullet chart: for each {{axis}}, "{{first}}" rendered as a bar compared against its corresponding {{target}} marker.
criteria.ladder: Quantile ladders: for each {{axis}}, a segment spanning from minimum to maximum across {{#list series prefix='"' suffix='"' join=', '}}{{this}}{{/list}}{{#if moreSeries}} plus {{moreSeries}} more{{/if}} with markers at each value on a common axis.
criteria.histogram: Histogram: {{#list series prefix='"' suffix='"' join=', '}}{{this}}{{/list}} rendered as vertical bars across the {{axis}} bins in bin sequence.
criteria.stat: Stat tiles: one summary card per {{#list series prefix='"' suffix='"' join=', '}}{{this}}{{/list}}, highlighting the ratio between {{#list rows prefix='"' suffix='"' join=', '}}{{this}}{{/list}} in prominent numerals.
criteria.none: No chart: the table communicates it clearly on its own.

worth.instructions: The input state is a Markdown table from a coding assistant's reply, along with inferred column types. Would rendering a chart beneath this table aid comprehension—specifically, does it contain numeric metrics compared across rows or columns that become clearer visually? Answer no when the numbers represent identifiers, codes, versions, parameters, indices, timestamps, or counts cited in prose, when individual cells bundle multiple numbers, or when values are too few or too uniform to contrast beyond what the table already shows.

metrics.instructions: The input state is a Markdown table from a coding assistant's reply, along with inferred column types. Does each row represent a distinct metric (with its own unit or semantics, such as "latency", "cost", "success rate") while columns hold the entities being compared? Answer no when each row is an entity evaluated across a consistent set of column metrics.

shading.instructions: The input state is a Markdown table from a coding assistant's reply, along with inferred column types. Imagine rendering every value as a shaded cell in a row-by-column grid. Which cells belong on the same color scale? Choose series when columns represent distinct metrics (e.g., input vs. output vs. reasoning tokens, recall vs. cost) so each column is normalized independently. Choose row when columns measure the same quantity under different conditions (e.g., stock vs. branch build time, c4 vs. c8) while rows span vastly different magnitudes (a tiny app alongside a massive one) so each row is normalized across its columns. Choose shared when all cells measure the same quantity on a comparable scale so any pair of cells can be compared directly.

criteria.shared: All cells represent one metric on a comparable scale; any two cells are directly comparable.
criteria.series: Columns represent different metrics; normalize independently per column.
criteria.row: Columns measure one metric across conditions while rows vary sharply in magnitude; normalize across each row.

order.instructions: The input state is a Markdown table from a coding assistant's reply, along with inferred column types. A chart will be rendered beneath the table, one bar/entry per row, plotting "{{column}}". How should the rows be ordered? Choose table if the existing row order carries meaning (chronological sequence, pipeline stages, size tiers, baseline first, grouped relatives) or is already sorted. Choose descending or ascending only when rows are unordered, independent items where sorting by "{{column}}" improves readability: descending puts largest values first, while ascending puts smallest values first when lower is better (latency, cost, error counts).

criteria.table: Preserve the table's row sequence: it is meaningful or already sorted.
criteria.descending: Sort independent rows from largest to smallest.
criteria.ascending: Sort independent rows from smallest to largest: lower is better.

reference.instructions: The input state is a Markdown table from a coding assistant's reply, along with inferred column types. A chart will be rendered beneath the table with one entry per row. Does one row serve as the reference benchmark against which all other rows are compared—such as a baseline, control, default, stock, or current configuration—so other rows should be interpreted as higher or lower relative to it? Select its "{{column}}" value{{#if repeats}} (it may appear once per group, such as each model's baseline run){{/if}}. Select none if no row serves as a reference: merely appearing first, scoring highest, or being recommended does not make a row a reference.

label.instructions: The input state is a Markdown table from a coding assistant's reply, along with inferred column types. A chart will be rendered beneath the table, one entry per row, labeled from a single column. Which column identifies the rows—the concise label a reader uses to refer to each row (such as a model, file, scenario, option, or thread)? Exclude descriptions, notes, verdicts, or yes/no flags. A numeric column serves as the label only when it acts as an identifier or index (a thread ID, finding number, or numbered option), never when it is a measured quantity being compared.

conditions.instructions: The input state is a Markdown table from a coding assistant's reply, along with inferred column types. Do the columns {{#list columns prefix='"' suffix='"' join=', '}}{{this}}{{/list}} represent the same metric evaluated under varying conditions—such as before vs. after a change, a baseline vs. variants, or different versions, tools, or setups—making values across a row directly comparable? Answer no when they represent distinct quantities (vertices vs. faces, share vs. rate, count vs. score, total vs. components or delta) or when the table simply wraps one list into two side-by-side halves.

column.instructions: The input state is a Markdown table from a coding assistant's reply, along with inferred column types. A chart will be rendered beneath the table. Should "{{column}}" be included as a plotted data series? Answer yes for a measured outcome that the table compares across rows. Answer no for sample counts or run counts behind measurements, statistical significance or confidence values (such as p-values), derived totals/averages/ratios/deltas summarizing other columns (e.g., a `ratio` or `speedup` computed from two plotted durations), nearly constant settings, or numbers serving purely as row labels.

name.instructions: The input state is a Markdown table from a coding assistant's reply, along with inferred column types. A chart will be rendered beneath the table, labeling each row from its "{{label}}" column. Should "{{column}}" be appended to that row label? Answer yes when rows sharing a "{{label}}" value are distinguished by this column (such as the harness, configuration, or variant used), so omitting it would make distinct rows look identical. Answer no for commentary, descriptions, or fields unneeded to distinguish rows.

group.instructions: The input state is a Markdown table from a coding assistant's reply, along with inferred column types. A chart will be rendered beneath the table with one entry per row. Should entries be grouped by "{{column}}", displaying each distinct value once alongside the rows that share it? Answer yes when other identifying columns repeat across its values (e.g., each model evaluated across harnesses), even if the table interleaves those rows—they will be regrouped. Answer no when its values are unique or the rows are unrelated items.

title.instructions: The input state is a Markdown table from a coding assistant's reply, along with inferred column types. The chart to be rendered beneath the table is: {{chart}} It takes a single-line heading capturing its core takeaway. Which candidate best expresses what the reader should take away—the key comparison or outcome the table illustrates? Favor statements spanning the whole table (every row improved, one option leads across metrics, one group clearly outperforms the rest) over isolated single-row facts. Pick none only when all candidates miss the table's point or are misleading.

criteria.none: No title: none of these options captures the table's point.

move.instructions: The input state is a Markdown table from a coding assistant's reply, along with inferred column types. The values in {{#each columns}}"{{this}}"{{#unless @last}}, {{/unless}}{{/each}}{{#if arrow}}, formatted as before → after,{{/if}} track a single metric across consecutive stages—such as before and after an edit, or baseline versus later runs—so each row transitions from one value to the next. Which direction represents improvement for this metric? Choose higher when larger numbers are better: pass/success rates, accuracy, scores, throughput, speedups, or savings. Choose lower when smaller numbers are better: cost, latency, runtime, errors, failures, turns or retries needed, and tokens, memory, or size that a change tries to reduce. Check headers, notes, and symbols near the numbers for polarity cues (✅ next to smaller values, "regressed" next to increases). Choose neutral when neither direction is preferable or the table gives no clue.

rivals.instructions: The input state is a Markdown table from a coding assistant's reply, along with inferred column types. A chart will be rendered beneath the table, highlighting the top value in each comparison. What are the competing alternatives in this table? Choose rows when rows represent competing options evaluated on common metrics (models, configs, benchmark arms, plans, tools), making the best row per column worth highlighting. Choose columns when numeric columns represent competing options evaluated across each row (implementations, settings, versions, or harnesses compared on each workload), making the best column per row worth highlighting. Choose neither when rows represent components of a whole, process stages, files, categories, before/after pairs, or descriptive listings rather than ranked competitors.

criteria.rows: Rows are competing options: highlight the top row per column.
criteria.columns: Numeric columns are competing options: highlight the top column per row.
criteria.neither: Components, stages, files, categories, before/after pairs, or non-ranked descriptions.

polarity.instructions: The input state is a Markdown table from a coding assistant's reply, along with inferred column types. A chart will be rendered beneath the table. Which direction is preferable for "{{column}}"? Choose higher when larger numbers are better: pass/success rates, accuracy, recall, throughput, speedups, or savings. Choose lower when smaller numbers are better: cost, latency, runtime, errors, failures, and tokens, memory, or size when comparing options or runs aimed at cutting them. For a delta or "vs" column, check what a larger figure signifies (a larger saving is better; a larger slowdown is worse). Choose neutral when neither direction is preferable: descriptive counts, sizes, shares, parameters, or identifiers.

focus.instructions: The input state is a Markdown table from a coding assistant's reply, along with inferred column types. A chart will be rendered beneath the table with one entry per row. Is there a focal row that the table centers on—the recommended or chosen option, the existing/proposed baseline others are compared against, or a highlighted entry? Choose none if no individual row stands out as the focus.

rowPolarity.instructions: The input state is a Markdown table from a coding assistant's reply, along with inferred column types. Each row represents a separate metric compared across columns. Which direction is preferable for the metric in row "{{row}}"? Choose higher when larger numbers are better: pass/success rates, accuracy, throughput, speedups, or savings. Choose lower when smaller numbers are better: cost, latency, runtime, errors, failures, retries, and tokens, memory, or size that a change tries to reduce. Choose neutral when neither direction is preferable: counts or sizes merely describing the workload, parameters, or identifiers.
